units.title: Static, dynamic and continuous batching and iteration-level scheduling
outcomes: Contrast static, dynamic and continuous batching, and name the drain condition each one removes.
Explain iteration-level scheduling and selective batching at the operation level.
Explain why a throughput-maximizing batch can harm TTFT, inter-token latency and memory availability.
units.why: Real request lengths vary by orders of magnitude, so a fixed batch spends most slots idle. Iteration-level refill is the mechanism every later policy in this section assumes.

next.note: Bound each iteration with token budgets and sequence-count limits.
Handle the prefill and decode interference that refill creates.

study.locator: Concepts 01 and 02 with the utilization arithmetic, the five-step iteration loop and selective batching; Math by hand Part 1 (a) to (d)

study.title: Orca iteration-level scheduling and selective batching
study.locator: Section 3 iteration-level scheduling with Fig 4; Section 3.2 selective batching with Fig 5; Section 4.2 Algorithm 1 iteration-level FCFS with max batch size and max_tokens reservation
study.depth: Skim the distributed execution in the rest of Section 4. Treat the 36.9x FasterTransformer throughput result as the paper's result on its hardware and workload, not a target.

focus: Slot utilization under static batching is mean length over max length, so one long request idles every shorter slot until it finishes.
Dynamic batching bounds assembly wait with a timeout but still drains the whole batch, so variable output lengths still idle slots.
Iteration-level scheduling admits and evicts at every decode step, which keeps the batch full regardless of length variance.

Selective batching flattens position-independent operations across sequences into one large matrix multiply and handles attention per sequence, which is what makes mixed-position batches implementable.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute slot utilization for output lengths [20, 35, 40, 60, 80, 120, 200, 900]: 900 iterations, 1455 useful sequence-steps, 20.2%. Then show batch 32 with mean 180 and longest 2000 gives 9%, and explain why growth moves it down: the max reaches further into the tail while the mean stays put.
traps: Calling continuous batching dynamic batching with a shorter timeout. Dynamic batching still runs each batch to completion; continuous batching changes the scheduling granularity to the iteration, which needs per-sequence KV management.

Assuming a larger static batch is always better. Utilization falls as batch size grows because the longest of more samples grows while the mean does not, and padding wastes both arithmetic and KV memory.

Quoting the 36.9x Orca result as expected gain. It compares against FasterTransformer on the paper's GPT-3 175B workload; your simulator should reproduce the direction and rough magnitude, not the number.

selfTest.q: A static batch of 8 has output lengths [20, 35, 40, 60, 80, 120, 200, 900]. What is the slot utilization?
selfTest.a: 20.2%. Useful work is 1455 sequence-steps and capacity is \(8 \times 900 = 7200\) sequence-steps.

selfTest.q: The batch grows to 32 with mean length 180 and longest 2000. What happens to utilization and why?
selfTest.a: It falls to 9%: \(32 \times 180 = 5760\) useful over \(32 \times 2000 = 64{,}000\) slots. More samples reach further into the length tail, so the max grows faster than the mean.

selfTest.q: What scheduling change removes the wait for the longest sequence?
selfTest.a: Decide every iteration instead of every request: evict each finished sequence and admit a waiting one on the next step, so slots refill without waiting for the batch maximum.

selfTest.q: Why can the QKV projection batch across sequences at different positions while attention cannot?
selfTest.a: The projection treats each token as an independent matrix row, so all tokens form one flat batch. Attention must stay within each request, since each sequence has its own KV length and positions.

study.title: Orca admission with reservation
study.locator: Section 4.2 Algorithm 1: `Select` admits at most `max_bs` requests in arrival order and reserves `max_tokens` slots per new request against `n_slots`, which guarantees its future KV fits

focus: WAITING holds admitted-but-unscheduled and preempted requests, RUNNING holds scheduled ones, and terminal states end ownership and free blocks. PREEMPTED returns to WAITING, never directly to RUNNING.
The token budget counts every scheduled token: one per decode sequence plus each prefill chunk. The sequence count caps live requests. A batch must satisfy both at once.

Nano-vLLM schedules prefill first and returns early when any prefill is scheduled, so decode-only iterations happen only with no schedulable prefill. Only the first waiting sequence may take a partial chunk.
Conservative admission reserves the full footprint up front, as Orca does with `max_tokens`. Optimistic admission packs tighter and relies on preemption, which the next unit covers.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, decide admission with a token budget of 2048 and at most 8 sequences: 3 running sequences hold 1500 cached tokens and need 3 decode tokens, and two waiting prefills need 1200 and 900 tokens. Admit the 1200-token prefill (\(3 + 1200 = 1203 \le 2048\)) and defer the 900-token one (\(1203 + 900 = 2103 > 2048\)). State both checks in tokens and in sequence count.
traps: Treating the two knobs as phase-exclusive. Decode tokens also consume the token budget (one each), and long prefills also consume sequence slots; either limit can bind in any iteration.
Reading `--max-num-seqs` as the running cap. vLLM admits at most `max_num_active_seqs` into RUNNING and parks the rest in deferred waiting, so waiting has more than one reason.
Copying Example 6-1 values as defaults. Installed v0.31.0 defaults vary by GPU class and context, so derive feasibility from the flags on your engine, not from the book example.

selfTest.q: What moves a request from RUNNING to PREEMPTED, and where does it go next?
selfTest.a: Memory pressure during decode admission: the scheduler reclaims its blocks and requeues it at the front of WAITING. It must be rescheduled and recomputed, never resumed in place.

selfTest.q: A batch holds 4 decode sequences under a 2048-token budget. How many tokens of prefill chunk fit?
selfTest.a: \(2048 - 4 = 2044\) tokens. Each decode sequence contributes one token to the budget.

selfTest.q: Why does Orca reserve `max_tokens` slots for a new request instead of its prompt length?
selfTest.a: Output length is unknown at admission, so only the request's maximum possible footprint guarantees its future KV fits. The cost is lower admission under uncertain lengths.

selfTest.q: Nano-vLLM has a schedulable prefill and free decode slots. Does the decode loop run?
selfTest.a: No. `schedule` returns as soon as any prefill is scheduled, so decode-only iterations run only when no waiting prefill fits.

study.title: Orca reservation against scheduler deadlock
study.locator: Section 4.2 around Algorithm 1: reserving `max_tokens` slots per new request so the K/V manager never deadlocks with no space for the next token

focus: Admission commits blocks for tokens that do not exist yet. Reserving the maximum bounds the risk and lowers fill; admitting on current length fills tighter and needs a working preemption path.
Recompute discards KV and re-runs prefill on resume. Swap copies KV to host memory and back. The crossover sits where one prefill costs more than the round trip.

Nano-vLLM only recomputes: `preempt` frees every block and the request restarts prefill from its tokens. vLLM v1 also preempts by recomputation; swap is gone, so size the reserve for recompute cost, not transfer cost.
Repeated preemption of the same request signals an undersized reserve or an overpacked batch, not bad luck. Count preemptions per request and treat growth as the alarm.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute the swap round trip for 2.5 GiB at 50 GB/s each way: about 50 ms per direction, about 100 ms total. Then state the decision rule: recompute wins when one prefill of the sequence costs less than that round trip, which favours short sequences, and swap wins for long ones where prefill exceeds transfer.
traps: Assuming swap exists in vLLM v1. The engine removed swap space and preempts by recomputation, so a plan that prices preemption as a PCIe transfer misprices every eviction.
Pricing preemption as free because tokens are reused. Recompute re-runs the full prefill and re-consumes its token budget, which delays every other waiter.
Reserving exactly the prompt length. Growth during decode is the risk, so the reserve must cover future tokens or the scheduler must be ready to preempt on the first append that does not fit.

selfTest.q: What deadlock does Orca reservation prevent?
selfTest.a: A pool full of running requests with no free slot for any next token, where no iteration can issue and no request can finish to free space. Reserving the maximum footprint admits only requests whose completion fits.

selfTest.q: A 2.5 GiB sequence faces preemption on a 50 GB/s link. What does swap cost, and when is recompute cheaper?
selfTest.a: About 50 ms each way, about 100 ms total. Recompute is cheaper when one prefill of that sequence costs less than the round trip.

selfTest.q: Nano-vLLM preempts a decode sequence. What exactly is freed and what restarts?
selfTest.a: `deallocate` frees all its blocks and zeroes its cached tokens, and the sequence requeues at the waiting front with `is_prefill` set, so it restarts with prefill from its stored tokens.

selfTest.q: One request preempts five times while others preempt never. What should you change?
selfTest.a: The admission policy, not the request. Repeated preemption of the same victim means the reserve is too small or the batch is overpacked; raise the reserve or tighten admission.
